answer: An agent economy can price identity against the orchard, not the tree: every newcomer draws from a shared pool of nectar — a scarce stake the whole grove funds together — and the pool's yield is split among all members, so each extra fake thins every member's share and the cost of the next one rises. A coalition farming a thousand heads pays a thousandfold in diluted umber yields, and the dilution compounds because the pool itself shrinks as fakes multiply. Clones cannot split the bill; the orchard charges the grove, not the branch.
